title: Impact of Local Qualifying Salary Requirement and Expansion of Progressive Wage Model on Costs, Productivity and Jobs
what_it_is: Impact of Local Qualifying Salary Requirement and Expansion of Progressive Wage Model on Costs, Productivity and Jobs

sections.label: Local Qualifying Salary and Workfare questions
sections.summary: Questions ask about Singaporeans earning below the Local Qualifying Salary, its determination, and lowering the Workfare Income Supplement qualifying age to 30.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) for each of the last five years, how many Singaporeans make less than the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS); (b) what is the breakdown by job type and industry for these Singaporeans; and (c) how is the LQS determined and how often is the level reviewed.

sentences.speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) what are the considerations for lowering the qualifying age of the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) from 35 to 30 years old; (b) whether the Ministry will consider extending it to lower-wage workers below 30 years of age; and (c) whether it shifts the financial burden from the Government in paying WIS to employers via the Progressive Wage Model as it becomes more pervasive and lead to rises in personal income.

sections.label: Employees under $1,400 coverage
sections.summary: A question asks how many Singaporean employees earning under $1,400 monthly will not be covered by Local Qualifying Salary requirement changes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Manpower how many Singaporean employees currently earning under $1,400 per month will not be covered by the changes to the Local Qualifying Salary requirement for companies.

sections.label: Progressive Wage Model support and Mark
sections.summary: Questions ask about transitory support for employers under the expanded Progressive Wage Model, PW Mark administration, and procurement encouraging the Mark.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) what transitory support will the Government provide to employers as the implementation of the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) is expanded, especially during pandemic uncertainties; (b) how will the Progressive Wage Mark (PW Mark) be administered; and (c) how can the public and private sectors through their procurement and purchases of goods and services, encourage more businesses to obtain the PW Mark.

sections.label: Support and safeguards under tightened LQS
sections.summary: Questions ask whether low-income families will get financial support and what safeguards prevent companies passing costs to consumers under the tightened Local Qualifying Salary requirement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Manpower in light of the tightened Local Qualifying Salary requirement (a) whether the Ministry will provide additional financial support to low-income families to help them cope with the expected increase in the cost of goods and services; (b) what are the safeguards to prevent companies from passing the entire burden to consumers; and (c) how can we ensure that businesses do not engage in such practices.

sections.label: Workfare spending increase
sections.summary: Workfare is the foundation of Government support for lower-wage workers, with spending about $850 million yearly, expected to rise to $1.1 billion by 2023.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: Workfare is the foundation of the Government’s support for our lower-wage workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: We currently spend about $850 million a year on Workfare.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: The Prime Minister has announced that Workfare spending is expected to increase to $1.1 billion by 2023.

sections.label: Real income growth percentiles
sections.summary: From 2009 to 2019, real income at the 20th percentile of the resident workforce grew 39% cumulatively, faster than the median worker's 33%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: From 2009 to 2019, real income at the 20th percentile of our resident workforce grew 39% cumulatively, faster than the median worker at 33%.

sections.label: Tripartite consensus on Progressive Wages
sections.summary: The Workgroup reached tripartite consensus on 18 recommendations, including significantly widening Progressive Wages coverage.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: The Workgroup achieved tripartite consensus on 18 recommendations, including significantly widening the coverage of Progressive Wages.

sections.label: New Local Qualifying Salary requirement
sections.summary: A new LQS requirement will make employers pay all local workers at least the LQS to access any foreign worker.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: Second, we will introduce a new Local Qualifying Salary (LQS) requirement where employers will need to pay all its local workers at least the LQS, in order to access any foreign worker.

sections.label: LQS start and low-wage numbers
sections.summary: From September next year, firms hiring foreign workers must pay all local workers the LQS; 103,000 resident employees earned below $1,400 monthly in 2020.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: From September next year, firms hiring foreign workers will have to pay all local workers the LQS.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: To Ms He Ting Ru’s query, there are 103,000 full-time resident employees earning a gross monthly income of below $1,400 in 2020, which is about 5.3% of the full-time employed resident workforce.

sections.label: Wage rise estimate under LQS
sections.summary: With the new LQS requirement, an estimated 77% of these employees should see wages rise to at least $1,400 a month.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: With the new LQS requirement, an estimated 77% of these employees should see their wages rise to at least $1,400 a month.

sections.label: Progressive Wages and PW Mark coverage
sections.summary: Progressive Wages will cover eight in 10 full-time lower-wage workers, and the PW Mark is expected to raise coverage to 94%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: The Progressive Wages will cover eight in 10 full-time lower-wage workers, and the PW Mark is expected to bring the coverage of Progressive Wages up to 94% of full-time lower-wage workers.

sections.label: No further LQS increase now
sections.summary: With companies still recovering from COVID-19, there are no plans to further increase the LQS now, focusing instead on implementation and wage benchmarks.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: We are also mindful and sensitive to the fact that many of our companies are still recovering from the effects of COVID-19 on our economy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: Hence, we have no plans to further increase the LQS for now, but will focus on the implementation of the new LQS rules and also for the other Sectoral and Occupational Progressive Wages to establish their relevant wage benchmarks.

sections.label: Public sector suppliers Mark requirement
sections.summary: The public sector will lead by requiring its suppliers to obtain the Mark.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: The public sector will take the lead and require its suppliers to obtain the Mark.

sections.label: Transition support and Workfare commitment
sections.summary: The Government accepted the Workgroup's recommendation for transition support, to be announced before September 2022 implementation, and will not shift away from Workfare.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: As such, to the queries of Ms Jessica Tan and other Members, the Government has accepted the recommendation of the Workgroup to provide transition support and is carefully studying the details of that support.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: This will be announced in due course and, certainly, I want to provide the assurance that this will come before the implementation of the first moves in September 2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: With respect to workers, I have already touched on the Government’s commitment to expanding Workfare.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: So, to Miss Rachel Ong’s question on whether there will be a shift away from Workfare to employers paying for the wages of our lower-wage workers, the answer is no.

sections.label: Transitional support and Workfare spending
sections.summary: The Government has committed to providing transitional support and increasing spending on Workfare.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: The Government has committed to providing transitional support and increasing spending on Workfare.

sections.label: 2028 sector wage end states
sections.summary: By 2028, cleaning and landscape sectors reach about $2,400 monthly, and lift-and-escalator PWMs up to $3,000 monthly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: If you look at the end state in 2028, where cleaning and landscape sectors will end up at about $2,400 per month, and moving on to, say, lift-and-escalator PWMs, too, going up to $3,000 a month.

sections.label: Workers paid beyond LQS
sections.summary: Most workers in firms hiring foreign workers are already paid beyond LQS, leaving the last 5%, with numbers affected by the COVID-19 pandemic.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: Most workers today who are in firms hiring foreign workers are already paid beyond LQS.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: We are down to the last 5% of workers and, actually, would have been much less, but the numbers were because of last year when we were down with the COVID-19 pandemic.

sections.label: Minority in non-foreign-worker firms
sections.summary: 23% of the remainder are in businesses that do not hire foreign workers, a minority of 103,000 full-time employees.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: In fact, in response, I did share that 23% of the remainder would be in businesses that do not hire foreign workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: So, it is a minority left: 23% out of your 103,000 full-time employees.

sections.label: Part-timer LQS hourly rate
sections.summary: The new LQS mechanism includes a rate for part-timers of $9 per hour.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: On the Member's second question on part-timers, if you look at the new LQS mechanism today, we do have a rate for part-timers, which is $9 per hour.

sections.label: Light touch LQS compliance
sections.summary: Firms will be advised on complying with the LQS rather than enforced against straightaway, with a light touch up front.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: Rest assured that while the LQS requirement may have kicked in, we are going to work on advising and seeing how we can get companies to comply rather than enforcement straightaway.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: That is why we have also given the announcement and heads up now, so that firms will be ready by 1 September next year to implement the new LQS approach.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: It will be a light touch up front.

sections.label: LQS purpose not minimum wage
sections.summary: The LQS is not a minimum wage quantum but exists to stop firms hiring phantom local workers to meet the DRC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The LQS was not meant to be a minimum wage quantum.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It exists to ensure firms do not hire phantom local workers to meet the DRC for the purpose of hiring foreign workers.

sections.label: LQS adjusted four times
sections.summary: The LQS has been adjusted four times in the last five years, from $1,000 in 2016 to $1,400 in 2020.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: To answer the Member's question, maybe it is by coincidence that the numbers are looking the same.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: But as I have shared, we have adjusted it four times in the last five years, from $1,000 in 2016 to $1,400 in 2020.

sections.label: LQS adjustments and Progressive Wages
sections.summary: LQS wage levels have been adjusted over time to meet managed benchmarks, with Progressive Wages guided by the National Wages Council.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: On balance, maybe, perhaps, it is coincidental, but the wage levels for the LQS have been adjusted over time to ensure that we meet certain benchmarks that we manage and it has been a fair one.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: We also have to manage over time and that is why we also take guidance for our Progressive Wages from the National Wages Council moving forward as well, largely because we want to make sure that it is sustainable and not open to political auction.

sections.label: Transition support for wage increases
sections.summary: The Government is studying transition support for employers for wage increases, and PWMs are negotiated with employees and announced years in advance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: The short answer is that, as I have shared, the Government is studying the transition support that we will provide employers for wage increases in the next few years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: One, we understand there will be some firms who are locked into contracts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: But overall, that is why it is also important for our PWMs to be negotiated with our employees, and, a lot of times, if you look at our PWMs, we announce them years in advance.
